title: Lidar Prices Fell 99.5%, and It Wasn't Volume — It Was Design
dek: Hardware cost reduction doesn't come from scale, it comes from design capability: only by shrinking a lidar that cost hundreds of thousands of yuan into a chip can it go from a feature part to a safety part, and finally to standard equipment.
why: Hesai CEO Li Yifan gives an oral history of 11 years of entrepreneurship, with first-hand details on pricing, fundraising, fighting for customers, and working with Li Auto and Bosch. High information density.
who: Hard-tech founders, people working in the auto supply chain, investors and engineers watching Chinese manufacturing go global.
skip: 12:05 to 32:13, the family upbringing and Silicon Valley work experience — low information density, skippable.

points.h: The 99.5% price cut came from design, not volume
points.body: When Hesai shipped in 2017, a lidar cost 200,000 to 300,000 RMB — as much as a car. Six or seven years later it was down to 200 USD, roughly a 99.5% cost reduction. Li Yifan's judgment: the vast majority of hardware cost reduction you see today does not come from volume, it comes from design — you get better at integrating things, and only after chipization can you achieve real cost reduction. He draws an analogy to Tesla: Tesla's biggest impact on the auto industry was not better automated production, but proposing a more advanced car design philosophy, cutting cost at the design level. So from 2017 Hesai realized it could not just be an assembly plant — it had to become a chip company at the same time. Today it has mass-produced its fourth-generation chip.

points.h: Three people split the equity evenly, and every investor objected
points.body: Hesai's three founders have essentially equal equity; Li Yifan is CEO but does not hold the largest stake. He says every investor objected, on the grounds that "three people shouldn't split equity evenly." His response: listen to everyone's advice, but don't follow everyone's advice — "listening and following are two different things." He argues further that once you need someone to make the call, it is essentially "a very low-level decision-making mechanism": the vast majority of disagreements come from different backgrounds and different values, and equity cannot solve those — even if the largest shareholder holds more than double the second, it still can't. A more common source of disagreement is inconsistent information, and that has nothing to do with voting rights; it can only be solved by designing a system and communicating deliberately. The three of them share one office.

points.h: In the first year they signed a 20 million yuan natural gas order
points.body: The first year back in China they were using lasers to detect natural gas leaks, and a customer asked whether the laser could be mounted on a drone for fully automated inspection. Hesai actually turned the laser into a fully automated natural gas leak detection solution, delivered with an iPad and a software system, to one of China's largest natural gas companies, for a 20 million yuan order. Li Yifan says signing a 20 million order in the first few months of a startup, at very high gross margin, felt great — but they soon found that this DNA didn't suit a very traditional business, and that it was only a direction a customer had suggested; nobody ever really turned it into a mass product, "it just stayed in that museum." The second year they did air quality monitoring, a few million in revenue, a team of about thirty, and by early 2016 they could already see the end of the road.

points.h: They deliberately made a 64-line unit into 40 lines to raise switching costs
points.body: The first product was called Pandora 40. At the time Velodyne was at 32 and 64 lines, and the most reasonable move would have been to build a drop-in replacement, but Hesai concluded after analysis that 40 lines was more reasonable — and deep down they wanted to build something different from the other guy: "I was afraid the reason you used me was that you thought I was a drop-in replacement." Li Yifan admits this carried a certain "literati arrogance": customers who wanted to use it had to abandon all their existing data, and switching costs were higher rather than lower — business school people would think you were crazy. His reasoning: the switching cost actually isn't high, and this is how you filter for people who genuinely believe in the product. On the name: the most Chinese elements are the five-star red flag and the panda, so it was called Panda, and adding an R made it Pandar.

points.h: The customer wouldn't let us publicize it, because we were the only usable option
points.body: Silicon Valley self-driving company Drive.AI placed a 2 million USD order and demanded the full amount wired in one payment. Li Yifan asked whether they could do a case study, and the other side refused citing an NDA; two weeks later, face to face in Silicon Valley, they gave the real reason: you are the only usable one, and I don't want anyone else to know — because nobody trusts Chinese brands, I took the risk and found you were usable, so why would I recommend you to my competitors? Li Yifan says that in that era he thought Velodyne wasn't good enough and wanted to find something better, found Hesai, so Hesai was his secret weapon. Around the same period there were also customers like Aurora and Nuro; 2017 revenue was about 30 million RMB.

points.h: There are only technology choices, not technology routes
points.body: Li Yifan says that in more than a decade Hesai has never used the phrase "technology route." He draws the distinction: a technology route means that once a company goes in one direction it can never come back, going further and further, one right and one wrong; a technology choice means what you do is something others can do too, it's just a matter of who does it better. As an example, he says the so-called solid-state and semi-solid-state are essentially just changes in the mechanical scanning method — they sound cool and make later players feel there's an opportunity to leapfrog. He offers an analogy: people making four-cylinder engines don't talk about technology routes, people making five-cylinder engines do, because that's an unreasonable design; once you've worked on it for a while and find the five-cylinder is a struggle, you go back to four cylinders and stop talking about it too. He acknowledges that the two choices — 90 nanometers, and multiple lasers plus a simple mechanical scanning structure — were decided under Sun Kai's guidance.

points.h: Not using lidar mostly means being afraid Musk is right
points.body: On the Tesla route, Li Yifan lays out a few facts: lidar is a perception method based on a different principle, and it will definitely make cars safer; it is not plan B but plan A plus — while A is executing, A plus is always working. He uses the analogy of a blind person: if you can both feel and see, and in a dark cave your eyes see nothing but your hand touches something, who do you believe? He thinks many of the people who are genuinely worried are worried that Musk is right, rather than looking at the data and concluding it isn't needed. He also takes apart the phrase "first principles": what Musk is actually talking about is biomimicry — the logic being that a human drives with only eyes, so a machine driving shouldn't need anything beyond that principle — whereas the essence of first principles is analyzing the most atomic nature of things without relying on statistical patterns; the two are the reverse of each other. Airplanes, he notes, are precisely the least biomimetic thing; Da Vinci flying the way a bird does was wrong.

points.h: Chinese companies going global need to replace the grab-the-money logic
points.body: Li Yifan says his biggest recent realization is that in new industries like cars and the auto supply chain, Chinese people are far ahead of most Western competitors — but "when you are clearly far ahead, how do you find a good way to get along with the world" is something they haven't thought through enough. He reflects that historically international business was a "grab-the-money logic": my thing is better than your local one, more reliable, sometimes cheaper, so please use me. That logic only works when you're very small; once you reach scale, in a mature industry what matters is — if you do business with me, what can I do for the local area, so that companies, government and the public all benefit. He mentions that Hesai has historically faced not only the International Trade Court and patent litigation, but also issues with the Department of Defense.

points.h: Hard tech has no network effects; it's a marathon
points.body: Li Yifan compares two generations of entrepreneurs: the internet is an industry centered on winner-take-all, where every battle is a decisive battle and you have to spend all your ammunition, because once the gap with the number two widens it never narrows again; this generation of hard tech has no network effects — no one has emerged who, like Baidu, Didi or Uber, becomes hard to dislodge once they're number one. It's closer to economies of scale. He calls network effects "a fairy tale of one era," and says entrepreneurs of that era had an extremely exaggerated winner-take-all opportunity. So the bigger problem for hard-tech founders is realizing this is a marathon — you can't spend all your energy at the start. He quotes Zeng Ming's saying, "look ten years out, think three years out, do one year," and says that in the early years he didn't understand what investors meant when they asked "how do you build a moat."

terms.def: Application Specific IC — an integrated chip system redesigned for a specific application, capable of being mass-replicated.
The US International Trade Commission — the body that hears patent and trade disputes; it is fast, and losing means a ban on sales in the US.
Proof of Concept — a customer first gives you a small project to verify your delivery capability before discussing a large order.

quotes.text: Because you are the only usable one, and I don't want anyone else to know — this is my competitive advantage.
In more than a decade at Hesai, I have never said those four words. Why? Because I don't think there's any such thing as a technology route.
That day I randomly asked a colleague, I said, tell me, what is first principles? Everyone's reaction was, we've actually never heard of it, we've only heard Musk say it.
I said if back then we were seeking statistics, we shouldn't have started a T1, because the historical success rate of T1s is far too low.
When I thought of America, I didn't think only of Apple — I thought of MBA, I thought of fun things.
Think carefully about where the industry's opportunities come from — they are actually the nation's, the people's opportunities.
